candidate.answerReason: The sum of distances is 3 between -2 and 1 and increases by twice the distance traveled beyond either endpoint. The strict upper bound excludes -3 and 2.

methods.label: Interpret the absolute values as distances
methods.explanation:
The quantities \(|x-1|\) and \(|x+2|\) are the distances from \(x\) to \(1\) and \(-2\) on the number line. Those two fixed points are \(3\) units apart.

When \(-2\le x\le1\), the two distances add to \(3\), so every such \(x\) satisfies the inequality. If \(x\) lies \(t>0\) units beyond either endpoint, its distances to the two fixed points are \(t\) and \(t+3\). Their sum is therefore \(3+2t\).

The condition becomes
\[
3+2t<5,
\]
which means \(t<1\). Thus we may extend less than one unit to the left of \(-2\) and less than one unit to the right of \(1\). The boundary points \(-3\) and \(2\) give a sum of exactly \(5\), so they are excluded. The solution set is \(\boxed{-3<x<2}\), choice A.
methods.levelReason: Number-line distances and a simple linear inequality give a complete elementary solution.

methods.label: Split where the expressions change sign
methods.explanation:
The expressions inside the absolute values change sign at \(-2\) and \(1\). Splitting there lets us remove both absolute-value signs correctly:
\[
|x-1|+|x+2|=
\begin{cases}
-2x-1,&x<-2,\\
3,&-2\le x\le1,\\
2x+1,&x>1.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(x<-2\), the inequality \(-2x-1<5\) gives \(x>-3\), so this case contributes \(-3<x<-2\).

For \(-2\le x\le1\), the sum is \(3<5\), so the entire interval is included.

For \(x>1\), the inequality \(2x+1<5\) gives \(x<2\), so this case contributes \(1<x<2\).

These three cases cover every real number. Combining their solutions gives \(\boxed{-3<x<2}\), choice A. The endpoints are excluded because the original inequality is strict.
methods.levelReason: The method uses sign-based absolute-value simplification and linear inequalities, with all interval endpoints checked.
